utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber is aware that the parties want to raise preliminaries. From what we understood, it would be about the Prosecution asking for one extra hour for the present witness. The Defence, not objecting that much, if they get a fifth hour as well. Is that a good summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue I wanted to raise was something different. Yesterday the Chamber asked us to report on some matters within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let me see whether this is also an issue apart from whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution had given notice yesterday that it was going to revise its estimate based on the pace at which things proceeded yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't object to five hours -- if you get five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is granted. Let's now move to the other issue you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday the Chamber asked the Prosecution for information with respect to the remaining bar table motions and 92 bis motions. So I provide the following information. The remaining bar table motions can be filed as the Chamber set out yesterday. With respect to Rule 92 bis motions for RM182, RM378, and RM379, they can be filed by the end of the month. With respect to Rule 92 bis motion for RM98, that was filed yesterday. The Prosecution requests slight variances in the Chamber's timetable regarding the other four witnesses mentioned yesterday. With respect to RM183 and 184, these are two witnesses the Prosecution has sought leave to add to its witness list. Once the Chamber enters its decision on these two witnesses, the Prosecution will be in a position to submit its motion under 92 bis in a relatively short period. For RM509, whether or not the Prosecution ultimately adduces this witness's evidence is dependent upon the Chamber's decision on a pending application with respect to the admission of exhibits through witness RM506. A witness who testified on the 12th of July this year. The Prosecution requests three days from the date of that decision to review the Chamber's decision and for the Prosecution to make its own decision whether the evidence of RM509 is still necessary. It may be that the Prosecution withdraws that witness. Now, with respect to the last remaining witness, 096, the end of September falls on a Monday, the Prosecution is requesting that the deadline for RM096 be moved to Friday of that week, the 4th of October. The attorney working on that application is engaged with other tasks at the moment. Should the Chamber enter decisions with respect to RM183, 184, and 506 in the near future the Prosecution would also endeavour to file any 92 bis motions for these witnesses before the 4th of October as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You earlier said for 183 and 184, relatively short period. If we would deliver that decision for example today or tomorrow or -- what is your relatively short period?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We would ask for the 4th of October then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might be a full two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there anything you would like to submit, either in response to, or in relation to, what Mr. Groome just raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just discussing with my colleagues. We don't know who is RM183 or RM184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to do that. And perhaps the Chamber could, perhaps later today, also give some clarity as when certain decisions, perhaps already very soon, could be delivered. That's because everyone is working hard on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this moment the Defence is not in a position to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. If after we have reviewed who the witnesses are and if there is anything you'd like to raise, please do so within the next day, not later than by tomorrow, I would say the beginning of the session of tomorrow. Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Yes, I'd like to put a -- something on the record. That is a follow-up concerning protective measures for Witness RM70. On the 2nd of July, the Prosecution sought the Chamber's permission to use the name of Witness RM70 in a letter. The Chamber hereby puts on the record that it made the necessary consultations, pursuant to Rule 75, and that the Chamber granted the request on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milovanovic. I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Groome will now continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, General. General, before I begin, I am concerned that at the pace we are going that I may not have time to ask all of the questions in the allotted time that I have. Can I ask you in particular with these next series of questions related to meetings and reports received by the Main Staff to give brief answers. At the end of those questions I'll give you an opportunity to add anything else that you think is relevant for the Chamber to know. Now, yesterday we were talking about the regular daily meeting and there was some confusion about who were the regular attendees at the regular daily meeting. Can I ask you to take the pointer that you were using yesterday. I've asked that the diagram be placed on the easel once again, and can I ask you to point to the people that attended the regular daily meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could it be turned a bit because the witness explained yesterday that he had difficulties in turning his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just maybe not quite so much so I can see as well. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please do that now?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There were those early morning meetings which were attended by the commander of the Main Staff. All the chiefs of various sectors. And they could bring an assistant to those early morning meetings, or if the commander so decided, the entire Main Staff could meet and that depended on the agenda that was to be discussed, i.e. on the problems in the various theatres of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if General Mladic was not present in the Main Staff, if he was in the field or he was out of the country, would this meeting still take place?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meetings would still be held even if General Mladic wasn't there. Then I would be in charge. However, sometimes it happened that neither of us were there, when we attended the meetings of the Supreme Command, it would be the most senior chief of sector who would be in charge of the meeting, who would chair the meeting. In any case, those meetings took place every morning and they started approximately at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just to be clear, who would chair the meeting when General Mladic was in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic chaired the meeting when he was present in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you said that on some occasions it was held more than once a day. Can I ask you to direct your attention to the period of 1992 and can you tell us with what frequency an evening meeting was also held, an evening daily meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those daily meetings in the evening were held as necessary. They were not mandatory. They didn't happen every day. But they did take place two or three times a week, and they were scheduled if the situation on the front lines so demanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we can think hypothetically, if there was a very quiet day where nothing really happened on any battlefield and there were no issues really to be discussed, would the morning daily meeting still take place?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those meetings were always held in the morning. That's when we analysed the plan of work for the previous day or we would discuss the plan of work for the next day. In any case, those meetings were taking place on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were decisions made during these meetings with respect to what orders would be issued to the troops?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That also did take place. Those meetings were mostly the place where we analysed the regular combat reports sent by the units for the previous day. Then the commander decided who should be helped, who should be assisted, which of the decisions had to be redrafted. In any case, those meetings were held regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My final question on these meetings: Can you give us some sense as to who were the primary speakers at these meetings, if there were primary speakers?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when he called the meeting to order, the commander actually introduced the issues that were to be discussed. I was the first speaker, as the Chief of Staff. I gave my assessment of the situation. My conclusions, after the assessment of the situation. I also submitted my proposals to the commander as to how to deal with certain issues and then the other assistants to the commander voiced their objections to my assessment or to my proposals. Then they added their own proposals or something of the sort, and when that discussion was over, the commander would make his decision and he would then issue tasks and orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to turn your attention now to weekly reporting meetings for the next few minutes. My first question is: When and where were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such meetings were held in the operations centre of the Main Staff. That was the biggest room in those prefabricated buildings. It could hold up to 30 people. As for the last part of your question, you lost me. I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When were these meetings typically held? Was there a particular day of the week or --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be at the end of the week, either on Fridays or on Saturdays. What we did, first we lined up the working maps of the corps commands with the map of the Main Staff. I would do that on the eve of the meeting and then I would tell the commander whether there were any discrepancies between the working map that was maintained by the corps command and the map that was maintained by the operations administration of the Main Staff. We often looked at the corps map based on their reports, and they did the same based on the reports of their subordinate units. There are often discrepancies in that exercise. When that is discovered, we then invite the corps commander to the Main Staff in the course of the week so there could be an alignment of the maps, so that all of the maps that we worked with depicted the same situation across the entire theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: These weekly reporting meetings, who regularly attended these meetings? Or, perhaps can I ask the question a little bit differently? Did all of the people who attended the regular daily meeting also attend the weekly reporting meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We usually called our weekly meetings as briefings, and the same persons attended as the persons who attended the morning meetings, plus the entire operations administration, from the staff sector, as well as the chiefs of the other sectors in the Main Staff, who also decided who they would bring along among their assistants. They had their subsectors and those would usually be the chiefs of the subsector. For example, there was the personnel administration, the mobilisation administration, and the chief of that sector could bring all of his three assistants, who were in charge of the respective subsectors. And as I told you, the operative administration attended those briefings in their complete composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was the agenda for this meeting different in any way from the daily meeting, and if so, can you describe the difference?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agenda for those weekly meetings or briefings were drafted -- was drafted by the commander of the Main Staff and he would convey the agenda to me on the eve of the meeting and then I would communicate the most interesting points to the chiefs of sectors. All of us prepared the reports that had to do with the work of our own sector. When the commander started the briefing, he would invite me first to give the assessment of the situation on the front line, and to give my proposal for the use of the military or parts thereof. And then if each chief of sector reported on his own sector as to what was done in the course of the week, what is supposed to be done during the next week, a discussion follows, and such meetings, such briefings usually lasted for an hour and a half to two hours tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were -- at this meeting, were -- or this briefing, as you describe it, were decisions taken and orders issued?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the briefing, the commander usually stood up behind his desk and he would then say, "Tasks," upon the proposal of the Chief of Staff. And then he added something of his own, something that he had already came up with earlier. At the end of the briefing, there would be seven, eight, sometimes ten tasks given by the commander. However, if a plan for a future operation was discussed at the briefing, then in addition to the tasks that the commander gave to the staff, the commander would also issue a decision on the use of the military based on the proposal tabled by his assistants. He would then say, "I decided" and then he would say what he decided. And then he would say whoever is opposed or -- whatever was said during this discussion would then become moot because we would all have to focus on the commander's decision and we would all have to follow through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you, can you give us a sense of whether Mladic's subordinates would have felt able to have engaged in a significant military operation, absent his decision or his order, with respect to that specific operation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the only one who could do that, if General Mladic was not anywhere in the theatre or if he was not in Republika Srpska at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if General Mladic was unable to attend either the daily meeting or the weekly briefing because he was away from the Main Staff, would he be briefed at some point about the discussions and the decisions taken by you at those meetings and briefings?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after the two of us met. Even if we had communicated another means of communications, I would inform him about the contents of the briefing, on what I had decided as his deputy. He would then either give it a thought or not, he would accept some of the things, he would reject some of the things. He would comport himself as a true commander. He would usually accept my decisions but he would always have something to add to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask you whether there was a briefing or meeting referred to as a monthly reporting meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be the last meeting of the week, because it was longer than the others, since the analysis of activities of the military were done for the whole month. It wasn't necessarily scheduled monthly but usually at the end of the week and it amounted to analysing the month's work. It did make part of the overall work plan of the Main Staff, monthly work plan, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who regularly attended these meetings? And again could I ask you, did all of the people who attend the daily meeting, did they also attend this monthly meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The monthly meetings were usually attended by all those members of the Main Staff who were present, whoever was on the location. Occasionally some of them were in some subordinate units and in different theatres. So there was no classification per se. Whoever was present attended the meeting, including the commander and chiefs of sectors, their assistants, desk officers, everyone save for the stenographers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this monthly meeting, did corps commanders also attend?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always, but when the Main Staff and the commander of the Main Staff made key decisions on the implementation of an operation, which touched upon one of the six strategic goals, we did so as part of the collegium -- commander's collegium meetings which included all of his assistants, that is to say all chiefs of sectors. And we regularly scheduled extended collegium meetings and it was the corps commanders who were supposed to attend such meetings to be present when the commander made decisions. That type of meetings was referred to as the commander's collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that I understand your evidence. There were two additional meetings that were held on an ad hoc basis and these were called the collegium of the commander of the Main Staff, and there was also an extended version of this which had additional people attend? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yet there was another type of meeting, which was the personnel council session. In addition to the commanders' assistants, we could also summon the subordinate corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the typical agenda at this council of commanders, I think is what you've termed this. What was the typical agenda at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At such personnel council meetings, personnel policy was discussed most frequently, such as the appointment of commanders, the appointment of certain assistants of the commander, if there were any changes in the Main Staff. Then promotion or awarding ranks to officers, implementation of stimulative measures, so to say, such as commendations, awards and so on. And anything that had to do with individual officers in the VRS. The corps commanders forwarded their proposals on promotion or measures of discipline, and such matters were always discussed at personnel council meetings of the Main Staff commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, do I understand you correctly that this would have been a venue in which disciplinary matters would have been discussed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the kind of forum where personnel matters were discussed. Personnel policy was implemented through this council as envisaged by the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If there had been an allegation that an officer had engaged in some improper conduct, was there a venue in which that matter would be discussed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that during the war because disciplinary procedures were in the hands of commanders of units. They were supposed to be in charge of disciplining their ranks. Breaches of discipline can be forwarded by subordinate commanders to the competent military courts of their region, and it could so happen that the military court would return the file to the commander, as their estimate is that no procedure ought to be initiated. In that case, the commander in question can discipline a soldier up to the level of a short prison sentence, since the state of -- since the state of war was never declared, we still worked under peacetime regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can return to the collegium of the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if would you allow me to ask clarification of part of one of your previous answers. You said the corps commanders forwarded their proposals on promotion or measures of discipline and such matters were always discussed at personnel council meetings of the Main Staff commander. On the following questions you said, more or less, that this was -- discipline was not discussed. Could you give examples of the measures of discipline you said were always discussed at the personnel council meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I misspoke when I said measures of discipline. The Main Staff commander did not decide on how to discipline a subordinate, because there were regulations in place for that. It was well known. A company commander may discipline a soldier or a subordinate officer, and could apply certain measures. The battalion commander could give seven days prison sentence and then the prison sentence went up the higher the level was. So I believe I misspoke when I mentioned disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you intend to refer to something else? Or was it just that you said promotion and then discipline was a total mistake? Or did you intend to refer to something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I wanted to mention, and perhaps this is what I meant when I said disciplinary measures. For example, the commander's collegium decided on removals of individual commanders, upon proposals of the subordinate commands. For example, a corps commander requested or asked that a brigade commander from his corps be removed. It is still a kind of disciplinary measure because it's a forceful removal. Someone was not doing their job properly and the brigade commander wanted that person removed. So it is a kind of punishment. That's what I had in mind. But I did misspeak when I said disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have a very brief question with respect to the collegium of the commander, both the normal and extended version of these meetings. During these meetings, would General Mladic take decisions about how operations were to proceed and to give orders?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander's collegium had a very strict purpose. The commander or the Main Staff through mutual daily or weekly consultations and briefings, reached certain conclusions. For example, an operation had to be carried out in order to improve the position of the armed forces in Republika Srpska. For example, in Operation Lukavac 93 the goal was to connect Herzegovina with the rest of Republika Srpska. The commander and I always had a thorough discussion in the woods nearby and then we would conclude that the collegium had to meet and at such collegium meetings the commander would state his goal that he wanted to achieve by summoning the people there. We always, or occasionally, called the corps commanders as well in the extended version. Since Lukavac 93 was to be carried out in the area of the Herzegovina, Sarajevo and Drina Corps, we also invited the other corps commanders so that the commander would put his idea to them, his general concept of the operation. As well as what he needs for that. And the other corps commanders not participating in the operation were there to listen. In this operation specifically it was so decided that the 1st Corps would lend two brigades, the 2nd Corps would lend one brigade and in the Drina Corps, a separate so-called combined Drina Brigade was supposed to be set up. So we would put the corps commanders in a position to participate in the process of decision making. The Main Staff can think up anything, but if General Grubac, the commander of the Drina Corps, says, I can't do that, it boils down to nothing. Then of course he had to explain why he couldn't do it. That was the goal of the extended collegium meetings. Every collegium meeting had a particular topic on its agenda, a theme. It wasn't like we -- that we discussed just about anything that was discussed at daily meetings but we dealt only with very specific topics, assisting the commander in reaching the best decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after this rather detailed discussion that was held at these collegiums, would, in fact, General Mladic then take his decision and issue orders along the lines of the decision?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two possibilities. First, General Mladic could do it immediately, at the meeting of the collegium. Thus concluding the meeting. But General Mladic was no robot. He would usually take time. He would say, "We now conclude this meeting, I will make my final decision tomorrow. This part of the meeting is finished. And a decision is to follow" at this and that time. So he needed time to analyse the proposals of all subordinates including the corps commanders, in order to come up with a vision of his own. Usually, all decisions pertaining to collegium meetings were made the day later because it were -- they were serious matters and comprehensive operations which required time. In the meantime he would even consult, perhaps, one of the assistants or corps commanders before reaching his decision. It could happen that a decision was made immediately but usually it was prolonged until he made a final decision when he would take the time necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, you've spoken about these several different meetings. My last question with respect to these meetings is the following. Can I ask you to explain to the Chamber your understanding of how these meetings contributed to good command and control over the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the commander would be given an opportunity to hear who thought what at such meetings, and then he would reach a conclusion of his own as to who was wrong or who was right. He would also take into account the different traits of his subordinates. He also took into account - he actually had to take into account - our positions, our thoughts. Commanders are usually abrupt, and Mladic, for himself, would usually say that he's easily jump started. But it was important that such meetings are not concluded with people being dissatisfied. Those whose proposals were not accepted were usually given an explanation why, either it collided with the situation in the field or in collision with the proposals of other commanders and so on and so forth. We had some radical proposals of individual corps commanders, which could simply not be accepted, and it would then be explained to them why it could not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, I want to now move to the topic of reports and I want to deal with written reports separately from oral reports. Now, yesterday, you said that on the 12th of May, you began to receive combat reports. So my first question to you in this regard is: Can you explain what a daily combat report is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daily, or actually regular daily combat reports had to be sent by every subordinate command before 8.00 p.m. That is to say, between 6 and 8.00 p.m. Such reports had to be forwarded to the Main Staff for the last day in written form. The contents of such reports were prescribed by regulation. First, it contained enemy information, in other words what the enemy did that day, did it attack, defend, make incursions. So overall enemy activities during the day. Item number 2: What he or his corps did that day. Attacked, defended. So the same thing as the enemy. Item 3, which we added later on, included information on adjacent units, our neighbouring units. But that is how we controlled the corps commands in terms of their ability to monitor the situation in the theatre. If the commander of the Herzegovina Corps reported that the enemy attacked the Vis feature in Srecko Polje, for example, the staff sector would refer to the East Bosnia Corps commander's report to see whether that piece of information would be found there, about the attack on Vis, because it was on the border between the Drina and the East Bosnia Corps. If in the East Bosnia Corps commander's report it is found to be missing, it means that one of the corps commanders is not following the situation. Or that General Simic, commander of the East Bosnia Corps, was unaware of the attack on the Drina Corps. Or the Drina Corps commander blew things out of proportion. And then the next day, teams would be set up at the Main Staff to go to the location to see who was right. So we made the corps commanders responsible for monitoring not only their activities but those of their neighbouring units. The next item, item 4, was the corps commander's decision for the next day, that is to say what was to be done the next day. Then we have an item on logistics supply, and first we would always have the losses, the killed and wounded during the day, the sick. That item was usually the most comprehensive one because it included commanders' requests for materiel for the corps. Then if there was anything in terms of morale and policy to be discussed, and the item following that, it could be skipped if there were no problems during the day. The next item was security issues, say something was stolen, there was a fight between soldiers, there were deserters and so on and so forth. Lastly, command and communications. Usually the commander would say, the corps commander would say: The command post, unchanged. Or a forward command post was established at this and that location. I can add by saying that the corps commanders could not relocate their command posts without an approval from the Main Staff commander. Forward command posts, on the other hand, could be designated by themselves alone in order to assist their units, but they had had to keep the Main Staff informed. So such were reports of subordinate units to the Main Staff. However, this doesn't conclude the story of daily reporting. Since in the armed forces, there is a separate term which specifies that reports have to be sent as from 6.00 p.m., meaning by 6.00 p.m. they should have received reports from their subordinates, brigade commanders. Brigade commanders had to assemble their information based on their battalion commanders' reports received previously. Battalion commanders had to tour the positions of their company commanders. So to cut things short, the process of reporting on the situation at the front lines began early in the afternoon and then from the battalion to the brigade, from the brigade to the corps, from the corps to the Main Staff. It would all take about three hours. We were supposed to receive reports before 8.00 p.m. From 3.00 p.m. to 8.00 p.m. we have five hours during which the commanders were duty-bound to report to their commander and to the Main Staff by phone, by protected line, that I mentioned yesterday. They would have to report that there were no significant changes in the meantime or that there were changes, and they had to be specific. However, they usually declined to speak openly on telephone lines and they would say, it is included in the report. So in terms of the meeting, the next morning, at 7.00 a.m., by that time we would have the reports of all subordinate commands. So this concludes the story of the subordinates' report. The Main Staff had an obligation, by midnight, to forward a regular combat report to the Supreme Command. A person was designated in the operations administration who was in charge of it. At first, it was the position of the Supreme Command to have such reports signed by the commander, but it proved to be too much of a burden because otherwise he wouldn't be able to go to bed before 11.00 or midnight on any day. Thus, that obligation was delegated to the Chief of Staff. And that is how we were approached by our subordinate units as well. So Karadzic would receive our regular combat report by midnight at the latest. Now as for the procedure of the Supreme Command and who studied those reports and received them, it was their own business. The Supreme Commander would probably receive information from that report the next day. And if he had a request for clarification, or an order of his own, he would announce it by phone to the commander of the Main Staff or to me, if General Mladic was absent, and then further measures were taken. So those are the two basic ways of reporting. I'd rather not discuss interim reports because I have included such possibilities in the description. There was another way commanders could report. It was in the morning before our meeting, before -- between 6.00 and 7.00 a.m. By phone they could report whether there were any changes during the night in their sector of the front or not. Since no one of the three armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina engaged in frequent night-time operations, usually there weren't such problems. There were of course incursions by sabotage groups occasionally but that could happen on any given side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, thank you for that detailed explanation. We have two minutes before the break. I'd like to ask you some very specific questions and if possible could you answer in a "yes" or "no" answer. You gave a description of the format of the report, the corps report to the Main Staff. So my question now is: Did the reports from battalion to brigade and brigade to corps, did they also follow the same format? Did they have similar information that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly the same. It's just that their contents were smaller in terms of text size.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What time of day would a battalion be responsible for having sent the report to the brigade? Can you just give us the time of day?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon, between 4.00 and 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What time of day did the brigade have the responsibility to send its report to its -- their superiors in the corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An hour later, so between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally the corps to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was between 6.00 and 7.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Between 6.00 and 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, would that be a convenient place to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would have one additional question before we take that break. You explained to us the reporting at the end of the day to the Supreme Command. And you said, I read from your testimony: "At first it was the position of the Supreme Command to have such reports signed by the commander but it proved to be too much of a burden because otherwise he wouldn't be able to go to bed before 11.00 or midnight on any day." First of all, I understood your reference to signed by the commander to be signed by Mr. Mladic. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's how things were, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, even if General Mladic did not sign that report to the Supreme Command on every day, would he still be aware of the content of what was reported to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I've already told you once, whenever there were any changes or whenever there were developments in the military, I would report to him on the -- and them as soon as I met him. Those reports that I sent to the Supreme Command would end up on his desk, as well as the reports by the subordinate commands, if it was my assessment that he should be put in the picture. I didn't send him all of the reports because he would have ended up with piles of paper. I made a selection and I only sent him those things that I thought that he should be aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But anything that was reported to the Supreme Command, the events on which -- the developments on which reports were based, were known to General Mladic on the basis of the meetings, discussions, communications, whatever, on the day preceding the sending of the late-evening report to the Supreme Command; is that how it went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily. It wasn't always so. For example if General Mladic was not in the Main Staff, if he was not in his command post, the staff would continue to function as if he had been there. However, I could not wait for General Mladic to return for him to look at the report, to sign it, and to send it to the Supreme Command. It had to be there by midnight. If General Mladic turned up in the morning, during the regular meeting, he and the entire staff would be informed about the reports that had arrived from the units and what the Supreme Command received as our report. If in the meantime, after the morning meeting and before the ad hoc evening meeting, there were some discrepancies or changes, we would discuss things either in my office or in his office. So he was kept abreast of all the developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We will take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom. Could I meanwhile seek from the Defence further information about whether they identified the famous 11 lines in relation to the 14th Rule 92 bis motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you seek information from us? But it's the Prosecution motion to include those 11 lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think yesterday I said we do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have missed that. I apologise for that. Then we add those -- those 11 lines can be added to the selected portion of the material submitted. I don't know whether that's already uploaded in its new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll verify that, Your Honour, and perhaps at the next break we can report on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so the court officer can include it. The court officer is instructed to do so so that the portions become part of the exhibit and I think a number still has to be assigned to it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if you're ready to continue, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I have a few very specific questions about the reports. My first question is: Did the commanders of VRS battalions, brigades and corps have the discretion to not file a daily report if, let's say, nothing happened on a particular day?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't have that discretion. They had to submit a report. Even if all they had to say in it was, "No changes," which was very often the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw you to what you refer to as item 4, can I ask you to explain, in a little more detail, what was item 4 in a daily combat report that the corps sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the corps commander's decision on future activities and actions. Usually that item stated that the corps would proceed pursuant to a previous decision. If there was a new decision, then its contents would be forwarded. For example, I decided that tomorrow I would launch an attack on location A, and I gave that order to my units. So this is where the corps commander actually drafts his idea, his plan. And those of us from the staff sector who studied those reports would first assess whether the decision was correct, whether it was doable. And before the morning meeting, or if there was something urgent in that report, I would do it immediately, i.e. by -- either by telephone or I would go to him. I would inform had him that the corps commander decided on something, but his decision was wrong because he was supposed to change either the target or the procedure or the composition of the units that would be engaged, and then the commander would usually respond by saying this: "Tell him, in your telephone communication after 2000 hours, that his decision was accepted," or "rejected," if it was rejected. But a sentence would follow after that: "In the course of the night you would receive our decision," the decision of the Main Staff, that is. And then in the course of that night, that had to be done, an excerpt from a combat order or a combat command had to be issued to change that decision and that would be communicated in a written form to the corps commander that issued the wrong decision in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask to you slow down a bit? Because I feel that the interpreters had difficulties in following your speed of speech. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I want to clarify something you've just said. You -- the record records you as saying that the commander would usually respond by saying this: "Tell him in your telephone communication after 2000 hours that his decision was accepted or rejected." My simple question for you is, when you say "the commander," are you referring to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the commander was the only person who was authorised to alter the decisions previously made by his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can now move to the oral reports. So earlier today you gave evidence that there would be a telephone communication, I believe you said around 20 -- around 8.00 in the evening and also at 6.00 to 7.00 in the morning and the primary purpose of this was to update the main command on whether there had been any change in the situation. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's more or less correct. And I was talking about any changes that may have occurred during the night, for example whether he came under attack or he attacked, which was rare. We're mostly talking about the activities that happened during the night and concern the infiltration of terrorist and sabotage units from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you said that Mladic would instruct that the corps commander's decision in item 4 be affirmed or amended, in a telephone call, would that happen typically in this 8.00 p.m. phone call that -- or this oral report?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, let me tell you this: When you start speaking, the sound is so loud at first that I get confused at first. Later on, the loudness is reduced but when you first start speaking it's too loud. And as far as your question is concerned, that would usually be communicated in that telephone conversation that we had after 2000 hours and that would usually be communicated by the commander, if he was at the Main Staff. In the conversation in the morning, before the meeting started, if there had been any alterations to the corps commander's decision he would usually tell us this: I received your written decision and I am proceeding pursuant to this. And in the evening, in the written report, he would be duty-bound to include that amendment or alteration in his report. Or if there had been any changes on the front line during the night, irrespective of the fact that he communicated those changes to us over the phone, he had to include those changes in his daily combat report for that day. Had he not done that, that would not have -- those changes would not have been recorded. Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Regarding the level of my voice, I'm standing back from the microphone now. If you still experience that loud noise, please let us know and we'll try to adjust the equipment, okay? This process that you're describing now, is this the way that the Main Staff was able to verify whether its instructions were given -- whether the instructions that were given were indeed followed by the corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first measure of checking whether the corps commander took those changes into account would be his regular combat report that he submitted in the evening, because he was duty-bound to tell us how he proceeded pursuant to the alterations introduced by the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who would typically answer the phone and receive these oral updates in the evening and in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, it would be corps commanders, who called the commander of the Main Staff. If the commander of the Main Staff wasn't there, they would call me. And the same was true of the evening calls. However, if I was the one who answered, if General Mladic was not at the Main Staff and they learned that, I don't know how they learned that, it would be the chiefs of staff who would call me. In any case, what concerned me most was for anybody from the corps command to report to me because the commander himself could be absent, so whoever contacted me, be it the chief or the duty operations officer, who was privy to the situation in the corps, it was all okay, as long as somebody called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My final question with respect to these reports is the following: You've told us in some detail the types of information that was communicated through these reports; I'm asking you now, was one of the pieces of information in these reports the amount of munitions that were used by a corps, the amount of bullets, the amount of artillery shells? Was that information that was reported to the Main Staff in these daily combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the daily combat reports, they were not duty-bound to do that because our subordinate commanders of various corps would submit to us an analysis of the operation once the operation was completed, and there they included the consumption of ammunition, fuel and so on and so forth. However, what they were supposed to do was to ask for assistance in materiel and equipment, and they had to specify what kind of bullets, shells, and other ammunition they needed. They also specified the quantity of fuel. They never skipped that. And if they said that they needed 1 million rounds, 7.62, then we would conclude that it was about one half of that quantity that he probably used in the course of the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would the Main Staff have been aware of the quantity of artillery shells that were being used by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always. From time to time, we did seek reports or when they submitted their monthly analytical reports, they would also specify that. They would give us the quantities. And your officers saw schematic of the ammunition that was available in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that was stitched to the working map. However, when it comes to the ammunition, the available quantities and the consumption of the ammunition was something that the technical service from the logistics sector dealt with. So whenever the commander had to know the available quantities or the consumed quantities over a period of time, he would receive that via General Djukic who was the chief of the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my final question before we move on from this topic: Can you say a few sentences about how this regime of meetings plus this regime of reports, supported command and control over the VRS troops?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I spoke about the command function in the VRS and I told you that it is based on several principles. The first principle was continuity which means that the command was a continuous exercise. The second principle was centralisation, which means from the top to the bottom, from the Supreme Command across the Main Staff to the corps commands. And the following principle was the so-called command relationship between the superior and the subordinate, or a senior and the junior. The most prevalent principle was the relationship between the superior and the subordinate. For example, General Talic was a Lieutenant-Colonel, and I was his junior. However, according to the principle of the military subordination Talic was not allowed to give me orders or to decide not to carry out my orders if the commander of the Main Staff was not there. In that command relationship, there was a formal relationship and a personal relationship. The formal relationship is what we saw on the schematic that was before us just a while ago, and that was about the chain of subordination or the chain of command, and the personal relationship or the personnel relationship is a relationship within an institution, within a command, within a staff. It is a personal relationship between General Mladic and myself, General Mladic and the other individual chiefs of sectors. The relationship between General Mladic and each of the corps commanders. This would be the personal relationship which reflects how much we respect each other, how much we value each other, and to what extent we adopt the following principle, and that is the principle of military subordination. Let me go back to the part of the sentence where I said that everything goes from the top to the bottom when it comes to command. When it comes to reporting, it's just the other way around, from the bottom to the top of the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, during the existence of the VRS, from the 12th of May until the end of the war, was there any period of time which, in your view, the command and control structure, that you've described for us over the last two days, did not function as intended?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a period during the final operations undertaken by the VRS, i.e. during the Croatian Operation Storm in the western front. The Supreme Command, i.e. the Supreme Commander, was giving me direct orders in Drvar, either by sending me telegrams or by calling me. All the orders that I received from him were forwarded by myself to General Mladic. And I waited for his position because General Mladic was my immediate superior. I warned Karadzic several times that what he was doing, that that way of issuing orders, was a waste of time because every time I received an order, I had to forward it to Mladic and then General Mladic would respond. Usually he would say "execute" but I would never proceed without General Mladic's opinion. And sometimes it took 24 hours for an order to be executed. I told you that I had warned the Supreme Commander about the waste of time that that constituted and that that was also a violation of military subordination. Sometimes he would justify his acts by saying that General Mladic was too busy and that he wanted to do it in his own way, to make a shortcut. General Mladic and I did what we thought we should do. I.e., I always sought General Mladic's approval before I proceeded. If not his approval, I at least wanted to make sure that General Mladic was abreast of the situation. As far as the relationship in the VRS, from the commander of the Main Staff to the commander of a squad in a corps, that system of military subordination, or the system of issuing and receiving orders, was never changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, I want to change topics and I want to show you two directives, military directives. Before I do that, can I ask you to tell us, in theoretical terms, what is the purpose -- what is a military directive and what is its purpose?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You started your question really good. What is a military doctrine, you said. A directive is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are translated to have said, what is a military doctrine. I didn't hear that to be part of your question. It was military directive, which Mr. Groome was referring to. I don't know where the possible translation problem is but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there was a translation problem. However, Mr. Groome started by saying, doctrine but then he changed his mind. Instead of finishing by saying doctrine he changed his mind and said a directive. However, I think I understood his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A doctrine -- or rather a directive in wartime, is the highest form of doctrinally ordering or directing the activities of any military including ours. Directives mean that there is a turning point in the way war is run. Either in one part of the theatre of war or the whole theatre of war. In principle, a directive is issued by the political board -- body that conducts a war. This means that something is changed in the warfare policy, in the warfare objectives, or something is changed in terms of temporal determinants. I told you it was customary for the Supreme Command as a political authority to issue such directives. However, during my proofing I also told you that our Supreme Command, i.e. the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, did not have enough personnel and it didn't have personnel who was educated to draft such documents. So more often than not, that would be the task of the Main Staff. The staff sector had to do that more often than not. The first version would be then sent to the Supreme Command for their opinion and alterations. Such an altered version would be returned to the Main Staff for the final processing. When it was finally processed, it would be sent to the Supreme Commander for his approval and signature. Sometimes the Supreme Commander could, if a directive such as was directive number 4 -- constituted a military turning point in the system of conducting a war, then he could --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, if I can interrupt you there, I think it looks like you're beginning to tell us about directive 4 so I'm going to call that to the screen so everyone can see that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 709 be brought to the screens before us. It is entitled, "Directive for further operations of the Army of Republika Srpska" dated 19 November 1992, drafted by Major General Manojlo Milovanovic. I note for the Chamber's reference that a teleprinter version of this document is already in evidence as P1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, once you can see this, the first page of this document on the screen, can I ask you, is this the document that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that I had in mind but I did not intend to analyse it. I just wanted to offer it by way of example. As to when it was the commander of the Main Staff who could actually sign a directive. This directive was drafted over a space of several days. The staff method was used. On the 10th of November, I told the Supreme Commander that we were working on that directive. We discussed some other army issues, and I told him that he would soon receive the directive number 4, and I asked him to look at it urgently. I wanted the Supreme Command to analyse it and sign it. He received the directive a few days later, a few days after the 10th of November. We even met on the 11th of November and he ordered me to wait for him in Han Pijesak. He was en route to somewhere in the north. And then we travelled in his car to Vlasenica and we discussed some military matters including this particular directive. The directive was indeed sent to him. However, one or two days later, the vice-president, Koljevic called us and told us that the Supreme Command adopted a directive, but since the directive contained very precise military matters, that the directive should also be signed by the commander of the Main Staff, and that's what was done. I told you that it was a political authority that issued the directive. In our case it was the Supreme Command. There were such -- there were exceptions, such was this directive, that were -- were also signed by the commander of the Main Staff. That was my intention when I mentioned this directive number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. You're talking about the document being signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the last page in both versions and take a look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you are able to see the signature, can you tell us, do you recognise it? And it's the signature below General Mladic's name.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber the circumstances under which you signed in place of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to tell you before I was interrupted. It is my signature. However, on the directive that we worked on, which was sent by teleprinter, there is General Mladic's signature. I don't know how it came to be that my signature was on this copy, because it is illogical. First of all, on the 19th, General Mladic was in the field and I can sign documents only when he was away outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So being in the theatre was not sufficient. You ran some checks and it turns out that General Mladic had negotiations with General Morillon at Pale around noon that day. Another thing which bothers me concerning the signature is this: You showed me the original of this document which has a purple stamp. It is well known that the archives -- that there is no archives of the Main Staff. Now, how could then this original come from the Main Staff archives? There is a possibility that, following the teleprinter processing of the directive and its sending to the units, the teleprinted part was typed -- retyped so as to remain in the archives of the Main Staff, because the teleprinter documents usually did not make their way into the archives. And then I signed it simply to have the document stored or archived. Still, what remains unknown is how the Tribunal has this original when there are no Main Staff archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Should the Chamber ever be interested in that information it's something the Prosecution can provide. General, you've mentioned that you had an opportunity to see the original. After having looked at the original, do you believe the document to be authentic or not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is completely authentic. I drafted it. Actually, I compiled it. It was drafted by all of the commanders' assistants. I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General, having looked at the original of the document, was there some text above your signature which you were able to see in the original that is quite difficult to see on the digital version of the document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Is it item C or D?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask the question in a different way. Did you have a practice, if you were signing a document for General Mladic, did you have a practice which you engaged in to indicate that was the fact, that you were signing for him?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is this word "for," but as far as I could see on the original, although I don't see it here, this "for" is in the Cyrillic script, whereas I sign my last name in the Latin script. And in the original, I could definitely see the letter Z whereas the A is covered by the stamp but one could infer that it is actually "for." If I had truly signed this document in its original, it would have said "deputy commander, Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic." So the word "for" indicated to me that Mladic was in the theatre. Now, why my signature is there, whether I did so upon his approval or not, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version be zoomed in on the signature block?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If Your Honours want to see the original, we could produce that in about 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, you were aware from other times that you have testified, that the interpretation of one particular passage in this document is of some contention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to e-court page 6 in the original and 5 in the translation and for us to look at that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The passage is from section 5 of the document, a section entitled, "The tasks of the unit." If we look at the passage beginning at the letter D, you see: "The Drina Corps. From its presents positions, its main forces shall defend with utmost persistence Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the general Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them and force them to leave with the Muslim population, the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas." General, since you are identified as one of the authors of this document, it seems only fair that I give you an opportunity to tell us what you intended by this particular passage.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This passage, from the directive, was used during my testimony in the Srebrenica group trial, between the 29th of May and the 1st of June, 2007. The discussion of this passage was initiated by the prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey, when we had an interview in Banja Luka on the 18th of October, 2005. Mr. McCloskey showed me the document, where this sentence, beginning with "the rest of the forces" was smudged by the toner used in its printing. So it was illegible. I asked for a clean document, and he said, yes, indeed, it is smudged, but he did not have another document. He could only produce its English version. He asked me if I would agree to his reading out the English version, and to have the interpreter, a girl from Tuzla, Danisa, I believe, translate it. I consented out of curiosity. The interpreter said something I couldn't agree with. I don't have the transcript of the interview now with me but she said something to the effect that the main forces should be used to defend this and that, and then that the enemy and the Muslim population should be exhausted. And then the word "exhausted" somehow ended up being as -- interpreted as "expelled" or "pushed out," and the whole sentence was then viewed as my intention to have them forced out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, unless you think it would be unfair to answer my question specifically, and perhaps skip this mistranslation of the past, the text now you have before you, the original text, my question simply is: What did you intend by that phrase, by that passage?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to say. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, during the war, wherever there was shooting, all of the population in the perimeter of 20 kilometres would start to move. Muslims would move towards majority-Muslim areas. The Serbs would cross the Drina into Serbia or to some other areas with a Serb majority, for security reasons. I don't know how Croats behaved in such circumstances but it is irrelevant in terms of this situation. We knew that there would always be population movement. The idea was once there was movement by the Muslim population, they would usually go to Srebrenica or Zepa, in that area, was to also have their armed forces forced out, together with the population. The intention was not, as you believe, to have the population expelled. The intention was to have the Muslim forces pushed out because they had committed horrific crimes before that time in Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you describe where the Podrinje region is with respect to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica is in the centre of middle Podrinje. There is upper Podrinje from Foca to Visegrad; the middle Podrinje from Visegrad to Zvornik; and the lower Podrinje from Zvornik, Bijeljina, the estuary of the Drina and the place where it joins with the Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, am I correct that this directive assigns tasks not only to the Drina Corps but to the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the East Bosnia Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the Herzegovina Corps? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This directive was a result of the Drina Corps being formed, and by virtue of this directive it was introduced into the system of defence of Republika Srpska. It came into being on November 1, 1992. We wanted to find a place for it in the RS defence system.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, sorry, I'm just conscious of the time, so you've answered my question. My next question to you is: Each of these corps was also responsible for a geographical region in which there was some conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each of the corps had their own areas of responsibility, which was -- which had its precise locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that this phrase regarding forcing the Muslim population to leave is not used in describing the tasks to be carried out by these other corps, only the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this directive, the tasks which had already been assigned to the other corps are merely repeated so that the Drina Corps commander would be aware of what the other corps were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 709 as the next public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00709 receives number P2217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask that P2007 be brought to our screens. It is a document dated 22 December 1992, entitled: "Raising the combat readiness of units of the VRS, additions to directive 4," signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while that's being brought up to our screens, is it correct that there were two additions made to directive 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The number of the exhibit, P2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to get clarification because I noticed before that the Prosecution is using documents that are not on the list to be used with this witness. If I can -- I can be corrected if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic is correct, and I apologise. This was a document that the witness brought to my attention just the day before he testified. And in fairness to Mr. Lukic, I will not deal with the document now. It's already in evidence and the Chamber can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no. I just wanted to check. I would like to be noticed if there would be more documents. You can proceed. I don't object.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe there are any. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the only one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, the document that's on the screen, is this a document which you brought to my attention just before you testified?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said that it was an addition to the directive. Actually, it's an amendment of directive 4, the first of several. It came into being because there was a need to raise the level of combat readiness of VRS to a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, the Chamber will be able to read the substance. What I'm most interested with this document is can you explain its relationship to directive 4? Did it void directive 4 or did it supplement directive 4?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said that at the beginning. This document was used to amend or supplement directive 4, because there was a fourth enemy to the VRS. You can see that it refers to the meeting of commanders of the NATO alliance and of the European Union. On the night between the 16 and 17 December 1992, they planned air strikes and a NATO intervention against Republika Srpska. They even worked on some details. When we learned of it in the Main Staff, and General Mladic was not present at that moment, we made this addition to the directive because Republika Srpska had just acquired its fourth enemy, the NATO alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we look at 65 ter 9807? It's a combat order signed by General Milovanovic and dated 15 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, when you can see this document, could I ask you to -- whether you've had an opportunity to review the document prior to coming to court?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the last page in both versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you can see this, my question to you is: Did you sign the document as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, can you tell us, this particular order, does it also supplement directive 4 that we looked at earlier?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 9807 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09807 receives number P2218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, before I move -- I want to now move to Directive 7. Before do I that, is there anything else of importance that -- regarding directive 4 that you would want to bring to the Chamber's attention?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I should complete my previous answer but maybe there is no need. During the testimony between the 29th of May and the 1st of June, the Prosecutor handed me again this directive number 4, with some stress being placed on the disputed part of text. However, in that copy of the directive, in terms of the words "the remaining forces," there was nothing there. There was a blank space. There was no more smudging. However, there was some shade that could be seen. I used all of my glasses and table lamps, even the light in the toilet place -- while placing it on the mirror. I managed to decipher the text, and Judge Kwon asked me how I knew that the Muslim population would move, and I explained it to the Chamber by what I told you, that the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina tended to move. I think the Chinese are the first who follow their army in movement, the French are number two, and the Serbs are number three in the world. And in this war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims learned it from us. Thus, they moved with their army too. That is my explanation, in terms of why there is this part of the text which says, "with the civilian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move to Directive 7. Would this be a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's the perfect time for the break. We take a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Milovanovic, could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Earlier today the Chamber inquired about the status of 65 ter 29048. This was in reference to the 11 pages. I can inform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 11 lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 11 lines, sorry, and I can inform the Chamber that that now is fully uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now the new version with the 11 lines may replace the earlier uploaded version and it is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A final decision apart from the 11-lines issue will follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just for the parties to know that the request this morning for -- the request this morning for the four remaining Rule 92 bis motions to be filed not later than the 4th of October, that request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution appreciates that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that Exhibit 1469 be brought to our screens? It is an urgent memo signed by Lieutenant General Milovanovic on 8 March 1995 forwarding directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Milovanovic, before I ask you questions on this document, the Chamber is very familiar with this document and it is already an exhibit in the case. Can I ask that we look at the first page in the original and the translation? Now, we can see what appears to be a transmittal letter dated 17 March 1995 sending a document attached to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. It purports to bear the signature of Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic. My first question to you is whether the signature we see is in fact yours?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the date is not the 8th of March, as you stated. It is actually the 17th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is correct. At the top of the document, just under the date, we can see the phrase, "Very urgent." Can you tell us what this phrase indicates?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the document was to be sent or carried immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The transmittal letter is brief and it says: "Enclosed with this document, we are sending you the directive for further operations. Op number 7. Confirm receipt of the above-mentioned directive by returning a copy of this document." Can we now go to the second page in both versions? And my question is: Is the attached document the one that you were transmitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just it's page 3 in B/C/S.
