utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous document was a cover page, or, rather, an order issued to the courier, to take this directive, which was in an envelope, to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. What puzzles you is the phrase very urgent, if the directive was issued on the 8th of March and from the Main Staff it was dispatched only on the 17th of March, you're probably confused about the difference or the gap, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just listen to the question, the question is: Is the attached document the one that you were transmitting? There is nothing about time or, et cetera, it's just is this cover letter about this document? That's the simple question. If the answer is yes, please say yes. If there is any other answer, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You anticipated my question. The document is dated the 8th of March and once again marked "very urgent." My question is: Would it be typical for a directive marked "very urgent" to take nine days to be transmitted to subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Very urgent" is on the cover letter, and on the directive, you can see "very urgent", and you're right, how come there is a difference of nine days between the two dates? In the original of the directive, it says: "To the command of the 1st and 2nd Corps," and all the other corps which are enumerated here. I suppose that in the first cycle of dispatching the directive, the 1st Corps did not receive it, the person who actually put the document in the envelopes did not see number 1. He only saw number 2. I suppose that the 1st Corps intervened or the operative in the staff discovered that mistake had been made because he was left with one extra copy. And that's why this phrase, "Very urgent" was repeated, meaning that it should indeed be dispatched very urgently to the command of the 1st Corps which had not received it yet by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now go to the last page in both versions? I want to draw your attention to the signature of Radovan Karadzic. And my question to you is: Can you tell us, do you recognise the stamp that's authenticating his signature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What stamp is that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp of the Main Staff of the VRS, not of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now the Chamber is able to read the contents of this document but I do want to seek your comment on a particular passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we go to the section for the setting out the tasks for the Drina Corps? It can be found on e-court, page 17 in the original, and 10 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the sentence with respect to the Drina Corps where it says, "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations"? And can you indicate when you have found that passage?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you direct me? Can you tell me where I could find it in the middle or at the bottom or at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm a bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you'll find it in the lower part of the first paragraph under the Drina Corps. Yes. It ends with "Srebrenica and Zepa." That's the first paragraph and the few lines before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me read it to you but again I would want to you follow in the original text so perhaps I will wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the last sentence of the first paragraph under the heading, "Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it assist you to have a hard copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The most efficient way to proceed would be for somebody to approach my desk and show me where to look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the ninth line under Drina Corps, the first linear ends. It is the last sentence before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'll read the passage and maybe by me reading it and having it translated you'll be able to find it. The passage I want to read is: "By a planned and well --"

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does counsel have any objection to me providing a hard copy with a mark in the side? Can I ask the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just handed you a hard copy with an arrow indicating the approximate location of the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the B/C/S has disappeared from our screens. I take it that it will be back in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "By a planned and well-thought-out combat operations --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. There seems to be a technical problem. Nevertheless, the witness has a hard copy. The line has been read over and over again. If you would slowly read it, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "By a planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Now, my question to you is: Would you agree that a plain reading of this sentence would lead the reader to conclude that the civilian inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa were intended to be the focus of well-thought-out combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A target is a military term, and it indicates a target that has to be shot at. The word here is similar to target but it's not a target. This means that the activity is aimed at worsening the conditions of life for the population of Zepa and Srebrenica and as a result of such adverse conditions of life, they would be forced to leave Srebrenica and Zepa. However, with your leave, I would like to proffer a comment on this combat order issued by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is a directive now. This is not a combat order. This is in the directive itself.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my next question to you is: Based on your military training and experience as a senior commander, do you have a view whether this particular passage in this directive is a lawful military objective?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Geneva Conventions, the civilian population is not a legitimate military target or objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again if you can apply the Geneva Conventions to this particular phrase, is it your opinion that this is a lawful or an unlawful order?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlawful, if it is an order, but this is a political decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So can you explain how this directive -- I'm sorry, let me rephrase my question. So you are saying that the text as we read it here, you would consider it unlawful if formulated into an order? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it is formulated into a combat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you explain what is different or how is it different if this same phrase appears in a directive issued by the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a political decision, because it was issued by the Supreme Commander. It cannot be applied to military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Why can it not be applied to military documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, as I've already told you, the civilian population is an unlawful military target or objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask that we see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I seek on two points, clarification? First, you said "it cannot be applied to military documents." What cannot be applied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This phrase that we have just discussed cannot be used in military documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Clear answer. Then earlier you said you'd like to proffer a comment on this combat order issued by the Drina Corps, and then Mr. Groome said this is a directive now, it's not a combat order. And then you said, okay, I understand. Nevertheless, irrespective of the characterisation of the document, would you still like to proffer a comment on this document? If so, please do. And then specifically focusing on these lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this document, and I'm repeating this for the umpteenth time, was issued by the Supreme Command. It was signed by the Supreme Commander. This directive should not have left the Supreme Command to go to the corps commands. It should reach -- it should have reached only General Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff. Based on this directive, General Mladic was to issue his orders, and I can see that he did issue directive 7/1 which was a legitimate thing to do. However, during the proofing, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a minute. I take it, Mr. Groome, that you will pay attention further to directive 1. I was just interested in your proffered comment on this document, and now you're putting it in a different context which most likely will been dealt with by Mr. Groome. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, you ever mentioned directive 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that that be brought to our screens. It is Exhibit P1470. It's entitled, "Directive for further operations, operative number 7/1" dated 31 March 1995 and signed by General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, could I ask you to take a look at this document? Did you have an opportunity to review this document prior to testifying yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you kindly repeat the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question was simply, for now, and I'll be asking you several questions about this: Did you have an opportunity to review this document prior to taking the witness stand yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the proofing, before I arrived in the courtroom, and I also had an opportunity to read it between the 29th of May and 1st of June, 2007, when I testified in a prior case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page? Can I draw your attention to the signature? And my question is: Do you recognise the signature which purports to be that of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is General Mladic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we can see that has been drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic of the -- is he a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, would you please refrain from already nodding what the answer to a question might be? Would you refrain from any gestures? And would you also refrain from communications with the public gallery? Focus on what happens in court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is Colonel Radivoje Miletic a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Miletic was the chief of the operations administration. As we could see on -- when looking at the schematic of the composition of the Main Staff earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that the same Colonel Miletic who drafted directive 7 which was signed by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you to tell us your understanding of this directive, can I ask you to tell me what is the operational relationship between directive 7 and directive 7/1? In other words, it would appear that there are two possible relationships. The first, that 7/1 would supplement directive 7 which would remain in effect, or, two, that directive 7/1 would make -- would replace directive 7 and would make directive 7 void. Can you tell us what is the relationship between the two documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive 7/1 was a directive issued by the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, which originated from directive number 7 which was signed by the Supreme Commander, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is the relationship between the two? Does 7/1 supplement 7 or does it replace 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One does not replace the other. Actually, this means that the elements of directive 7 were now being used by lower units. Unit commanders could not take any measures based on anything that they received from Karadzic, and I said that it was a mistake on the part of the Supreme Command, when they sent the directive to all the corps commands. They should have sent it only to General Mladic. This was an instance of duality, or double lines, in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, when you say they should have sent it only to General Mladic in the last document, wasn't it you that sent it on? Wasn't it your signature on the transmittal letter?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My signature on the cover letter was only an instruction to the courier to take it where he was supposed to, but I was not even supposed to be aware of the contents of the envelope. I'm not accusing Karadzic's administration. Corps commanders should not have reacted to Karadzic's directive before receiving Mladic's orders as a result of the directive. I believe that only one corps commander did that. That was the Drina Corps commander, who did not wait for Mladic's directive that was issued and I don't know how much later, how many days later -- based on Karadzic's directive issued his order for defence or some such order, I don't know what it was. So when he received Mladic's directive, he could no longer react, and insofar as I studied both documents, in his directive, General Mladic omitted the sentence that we just discussed, where it says that the life for the civilian population of Zepa and Srebrenica should be rendered unbearable or something like that, whereas General Zivanovic literally copied that sentence from Karadzic's directive. When that directive was discussed, one of the lawyers put a question to me as to how General Mladic dared omit that sentence from his own directive and I answered him that General Mladic assumed responsibility when he decided not to put pressure on the population and not to adopt every single element from Karadzic's directive. He assumed that responsibility. He took it upon himself not to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question was whether it was your signature. You answered that by one word, yes. We are not here in a debating club where you present positions. You are here to answer questions. I, by the way, have one question for you in this respect. Who ordered you to send the transmittal letter? On whose instructions did you send it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was standard practice in the regulations. All transmittal letters accompanying mail to the subordinate units are signed by the most senior general in the Main Staff at that moment. That was my task because I happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier told us that if you received any instruction from the Supreme Command, that you would never do anything until you would have consulted with Mr. Mladic whether he agreed with that, "yes" or "no". Now, here apparently, something arrives which is to be distributed, you sign a distribution letter, you tell us that this was not how it should have been because the Supreme Command should not give any direct instructions to the lower level. Could you explain why, on whose authority, you did send that distribution letter, that cover letter, with the directive attached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The signing of the accompanying letter was not an order from the Supreme Command. I guess Colonel Miletic brought the sealed envelope, as well as the cover letter for me to sign so that the courier could lawfully go to the 1st Corps command. It had nothing to do with the Supreme Command or with General Mladic. It was Main Staff mail sent to a subordinate command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever Miletic would give you to be distributed, you would just send it and say, this is mail? Is that your position? Sealed envelopes, whatever the content would be, just send it down the line without even bothering about content?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite. On the envelope, it said directive number 7, the addressee was the 1st Krajina Corps. Miletic explained to me that this particular corps had not received it, whereas the others had, and that it was an extraordinary situation to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you explained to us that directives were issued by the political body, by the Supreme Command. Have you verified whether General Mladic agreed with this distribution, as you earlier told us you would always do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall whether General Mladic was in the Main Staff or whether I asked him anything. It's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier explained that it would only cause delays if you would receive something directly from the Supreme Command because you would not take action unless and up till the moment that you had the approval of General Mladic. That's what you told us quite extensively. Could you explain what happened here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not an order of the Supreme Command, this transmittal letter. It was produced in the office from which the directives were supposed to be sent to the different corps. They skipped the 1st Corps and I don't know on whose request. Miletic did find a copy of that directive, put it in an envelope, sealed it, gave me the transmittal letter to sign, and then dispatched a courier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you didn't know what was in it, apart from that there was a directive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew it was directive number 7 by the Supreme Command because it said so on the envelope and Miletic told me what it was. He said that a copy was omitted in the first round and that it was to be sent to that particular corps. I don't know whether the 1st Corps command intervened and requested it or if it happened on someone else's request, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And content of the directive was known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't familiar with the content of the directive. I wasn't familiar with it being produced. I didn't even know people were working on it, because between the 6th and the 12th of March, I was on the western front between Krupa and Drvar. When I came back, the directive had already been signed and put in envelopes. Even if I had been aware of the contents of that directive, there is nothing I could have changed in it because Karadzic had signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I want to take you back to something you said a few minutes ago. You said that General Mladic -- when comparing the difference between directive 7 and 7/1, you said General Mladic omitted not to put this phrase which you have characterised as unlawful, and you said, "He took it upon himself not to do that," in reference to removing that from the directive 7. My question to you is: Is it your evidence that Mladic's failure to include that particular phrase was an intentional act by him not to advance that particular part of directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my assessment, or conclusion, that General Mladic took over responsibility for not implementing that part of the Supreme Commander's directive, since he deemed it was unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there anything in 7/1 which explicitly rescinds that part of directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. That sentence was simply omitted from Mladic's directive to his subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, after directive 7/1 was issued, was the complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa still a military objective?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The physical separation of Srebrenica and Zepa at Mount Susica, had been our military goal ever since the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa have been established -- had been established because the Muslim soldiers and civilians kept going through the Drina canyon to the east of Mount Susica between Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'm not so much interested in the reasons why that was a military objective. But directive 7 says the following: "Complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible." I'm going to ask over the break that you take a look at directive 7/1 and see is there any where in 7/1 that Mladic mentions that? And I would suggest to you that upon reading it you'll see that that's also omitted from 7/1. If after reading that, you verify what I've just suggested to you, can I ask you: How would a subordinate commander have been able to tell that the order to physically separate Srebrenica and Zepa had not been rescinded but the order to target civilians had?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not understand the question. That first sentence, about exerting pressure on the civilians, that's fine. It's not to be found in Mladic's directive. I have to go back again to the Drina Corps commander's order. We find it in his order which means he copies Karadzic's directive. As regards the separation of Srebrenica and Zepa, it was a standing idea ever since the enclaves were formed, and perhaps General Mladic found it unnecessary to reiterate because we constantly had this problem of troops moving between Srebrenica and Zepa and according to the demilitarisation agreement pertaining to the two settlements they were not supposed to have been in contact. It was supposed to be overseen by UNPROFOR and not the VRS. However, since UNPROFOR did not do that throughout the war, the VRS took upon itself to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you over the break to reread 7/1 and I will come back to this at that time. I want to move on to a different topic, the topic of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile ask another question? You have explained to us that 7/1 contains a -- if I understood you well -- an instruction or directive, whatever you call it, which was, as you explained, was obviously illegal. Now, if you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but I believe he was referring to directive 7 not directive 7/1 as you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I made a mistake there. Directive 7 contains a clearly -- lines which are clearly illegal, as you said, from a military point of view, that is, making the civilian population an object rather than a -- it not being a military target. Now, you told us that in 7/1, this was left out on purpose because General Mladic did not want to take responsibility for such a line. Now, the awareness that directive 7 had been distributed to the lower levels, should not a strong protest or a strong line saying, "Whatever you read in 7, which was illegal, such as this and this and this, ignore that because it is against the laws of warfare," rather than to silently leave it as it is and that everyone should understand that whatever they received earlier would not apply any further because it was not repeated? Do you have any comment on those observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said already that General Mladic took upon himself, at his own responsibility, to omit the unlawful sentence. He was not under an obligation to direct his subordinates' attention to the unlawful nature of it because based on Karadzic's directive he issued his own simply omitting that. The subordinates are duty-bound to implement Mladic's directive, not Karadzic's. That is why I said at the beginning that it was Karadzic's administration mistake to have sent it to all of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you also told us that 7 was not replaced by 7/1. It was still in existence. You knew, or at least it was known, that it had been distributed to the lower levels, and then you say, well, it's enough to omit it. And you say you assumed that -- you concluded that it was omitted for that purpose whereas you now say again that you said already that he took it upon himself to omit the unlawful sentence, whereas earlier you said that you concluded without giving a basis for your -- the knowledge on which you base such a conclusion. Any further comments on those points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I repeat that it is only my conclusion, my presumption, that that was Mladic's reasoning. I can't say that he did so because of that. It is my conclusion that he took over responsibility not to implement or not to carry further that part of Karadzic's directive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He never told you, you never discussed it with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome. Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question? Did you discuss this question with Colonel Miletic, who was your deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw this directive for the first time in the Tribunal building sometime around the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the communication between the drafter of directive 7/1, Colonel Miletic, and the commander, Ratko Mladic, took place without involving you in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was done completely without me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, so that the Chamber understands -- I think it's important for the Chamber to understand where you were at this time. I'd ask you not to go into a detailed explanation of what you were doing or where -- why you were where you were but simply tell the Chamber: Was there a period of time that you were not physically present in the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 29th of October, 1994, until, I think, the 15th of October 1995, I was in charge of the western theatre, and I was in the area of Bihac, Petrovac, Drvar, Glamoc, Banja Luka. I omitted Mrkonjic Grad. Occasionally I came to the Main Staff for meetings or when summoned personally by General Mladic, such as when we saw General Zivanovic off or when we had analyses of combat readiness of the VRS. I think it was on the 29th of January, if I'm not mistaken. I was also there in late March and early April, before Operation Flash on the Croatian side began, and then I went to Gradiska where I was until 12 May. When I returned to the Main Staff, I found a telegram which was a request of the 2nd Krajina Corps, General Tomanic's message telling me that I should go to the western theatre because the so-called Carter's truce was violated. I hesitated but a decision was made and I left on 29 May where I remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to switch to the topic of Sarajevo. Was there a period of time that General Mladic was primarily stationed in Sarajevo in an effort to establish the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was immediately following the decision on the establishment of armed forces. General Mladic and Colonel Tolimir spent a month or a month and a half in Sarajevo at Lukavica where they worked on the issue of establishing the SRK. That is to say the translation of the command of the 4th JNA Army into the SRK command. We communicated by phone or by courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, would this mean that General Mladic was physically present in the Sarajevo area from about mid-May of 1992 to mid-June 1992 and perhaps the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that 65 ter 14730 be brought to our screens? It is an order issued on 7 February 1994 and signed by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, the copy of this order that is going to be brought before you is a teleprinter copy, it does not bear your signature. After you have familiarised yourself with the document, can I ask you whether you indeed did issue this order?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this order is addressed to all of the corps including the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to order number 2. It reads, "Rule out any possibility of uncontrolled shelling. Impose the most severe penalty immediately for uncontrolled behaviour or offences." Now, this order was issued by you within a few days of two notorious shelling incidents charged in this indictment as schedule G.7 and G.8. G.7 was an event in which three mortar shells landed in Dobrinja and G.8 is the first time a shell landed on Markale market. This order was issued two days after the Markale market shelling. My question is whether or not you issued this order in response to one or both of those shellings.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither. I issued this order based on the order of the Supreme Commander, number 01278 and so on and so forth dated the 7th of February. By the time I received it in the Main Staff, I had it translated into my own order and sent it to these corps commands, to the Sarajevo command for implementation and other corps commands for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, your order threatens to impose the most severe penalties for uncontrolled shelling. My question is: Can you recall any incident of uncontrolled shelling after which such most severe penalties were imposed on those VRS soldiers responsible?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall any. It was not in my department. It was within General Gvero's purview, who was the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs. I did not receive information from the corps in terms of whether someone was disciplined, tried or anything of the sort. I did not receive such feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was your assessment of the level of uncontrolled shelling, that is shelling not pursuant to an order, by Sarajevo-Romanija Corps members around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "uncontrolled", I would prefer to use the term "unselectively" meaning targeting areas and settlements without a stipulated military target or trying to engage a military target by shelling areas where civilians suffer. This order precisely requests that fire can be opened only on detected military targets or military assets possessed by the enemy engaging our forces. There is also a ratio, a shell for a shell, meaning that if one mortar shell came from the yard around the Kosevo hospital, they cannot respond with more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I take from your answer that there were instances where areas were targeted and settlements were targeted without a particular military target? That that was one of the problems you were seeking to address with this order?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any such case. I stress again that this order came as a result of the Supreme Commander's order. I don't know whether he had any further insight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be a convenient place to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but again before we take the break I would have one very short question, please a short answer as well. When you signed the cover letter by which the directive 7 was contributed, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my office. Miletic brought it for me to sign, since the courier was supposed to leave for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were at the Main Staff headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we break can I simply tender 65 ter 14730 as the next exhibit, public?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14730 receives number P2219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2219 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a clean copy of directive 7/1 in the original language if it's acceptable for the witness to have access to this during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he can read it over the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to read the directive over the break. Could the usher assist in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I also need directive number 7 so as to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Directive 7 I believe is sitting on the desk next to him if he be allowed to take that from the courtroom as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I take it that there is no need to inspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be given to the witness. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, I've been a bit unfair to you today where you said I cannot immediately respond on the deadlines, 4th of October, and then I gave a ruling that it was granted. That is unfair. If there is any reason to revisit those time limits, you have an opportunity to do so and we will then consider whether the decision should stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Time limits are never of our concern. We never object to any extension of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, if you would have said this this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what else to look into. I didn't know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the matter stands as it is, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the witness's last answer, about P2219, he made reference to an order by Radovan Karadzic. I just want to bring to the Chamber's attention that is 65 ter 14456 and it's the subject of the bar table motion for Sarajevo documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for giving us this guidance. At the end of this session I would need a couple of minutes to read a short decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, Judge Fluegge has one follow-up question from before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. Milovanovic, you said this is to be found on page 65, line 8, you said, "The term 'uncontrolled' I would prefer to use the term 'unselectively,' meaning targeting areas and settlements without a stipulated military target." Why are you now using the term "unselectively" instead of "uncontrolled"? Uncontrolled, we saw in the document which was signed by you. Why are you now preferring another term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason is simple. Uncontrolled means opening fire without a prior order or being held accountable for opening that fire. Unselectively means that there is an order but the fire does not focus on a military target but, rather, it is dispersed across an area. Non-selectively means to open fire, it is a military term, but that fire is not selectively targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is well understood. But in the document you used the term "uncontrolled."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that I copied that from Karadzic's order, or, rather the operative who was working on the text, his initials are MDj, I don't know who that may have been, it could have been Mico Djapa [phoen]. We had two men with those initials, one was Milos Djurdjic but at the time this was drafted Mr. Djurdjic was not a member of the Main Staff so it was probably Lieutenant-Colonel Mico Djapa who drafted that. When we discussed that document in the prosecutor's office, my objection was that I would not have used the term the strictest laws. This is not even a military term. A law, an act, cannot be strict or stricter or the strictest. An act is an act. This person who drafted this document must have had in his mind to emphasise that whoever breaks this rule would suffer the severest of penalties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I might help with the translation issue here and that's why there is confusion, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have that document on the screen that would help both you and the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is now P2219.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think you are referring to number 2, rule out any possibility of uncontrolled shelling. In B/C/S, I will read so you get proper translation. I quote: [Interpretation] "Rule out any possibility of shelling beyond control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Still I would like to know from the witness if he signed this document without thinking about using this or the other term, because it was prepared by somebody else. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. I focused on this ratio one for one, one shell here, one shell there. This said a lot to me. I'm afraid I did not pay much attention to the linguistics of the document. The most important thing for me was for the document not to lose its meaning, its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all from my side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to look at a video now, and then I'll ask you some questions after it. This is 65 ter 22344.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The 21st Sabotage Detachment has realised and demonstrated in practice the use of artillery for sabotage purposes. The 21st Sabotage Detachment was the first to use a mobile rocket launcher in combat. Go. The strength of the detachment's fire power is shown by the possibility to launch 18, 250 kilogram bombs in one fifth second burst of fire as well as 152, 57 millimetre rockets."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what munition we just observed being assembled and fired in 22344?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything on the screen. Can I start answering your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you heard my question. Did you hear my question - whether you could tell us what munition that was and if you would like us to try to put that up again?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need to show it again. I saw this video-clip when it was shown to me by you during the proofing. And that was the first time I saw it. I know that aerial bombs were being launched and what the speaker, the commentator, is saying about 57 millimetre rockets, I haven't a clue what he's talking about. I know that there were some anti-aircraft howitzers that were 57 millimetre so I don't know. I don't think that this belongs to the Army of Republika Srpska but to the 21st Sabotage Detachment of the Serbian Army of Krajina, i.e. of the 21st Detachment of the Serbian Army of Krajina. Some operation group. It's mentioned here. I don't know anything about that operation. I can only assume that those were aerial bombs that we could see in action and that their weight is 250 kilos. In our military, I never saw any such thing. There were no such assets in our army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the munition that we saw on the screen here, you're saying that there was no such munition in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any such assets or a launcher that could launch four aerial bombs at the same time. We didn't have such a system, and I don't believe, when the commentator says that in the space of five seconds, it could launch 18 such bombs, those bombs weigh 250 kilograms, you know what power and what weight we are talking about? I think it's a bit of an exaggeration, in the space of five seconds you can hardly launch one such projectiles let alone 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you first to focus on the question? It is what you saw. What the comments was is a different matter. And the simple question is: Do I understand that you -- the munition you saw did not exist in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The munition that we saw existed in the VRS. Those were lethal assets that belonged to the anti-aircraft defence and the air force. These are lethal assets that are usually carried by an aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's the simple question -- the simple answer now is one quite different from the answer you gave, which is -- Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the phrase "skalamerija"? That's s-k-a-l-a-m-e-r-i-j-a.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain what that phrase referred to when used in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a makeshift device to transport aerial bombs from the firing position to a target. So instead of using an aircraft to launch it, they are launched from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we now take a look at 65 ter 1986. It's a letter addressed to the chief of the Yugoslav Army from Ratko Mladic dated 31 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, my simple question to you now when it first comes on the screen is whether you recognise the document and whether you've had a chance to review this document in the week or the few days before you testified.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you saw this document, did it remind you of a conversation that you had with General Momcilo Perisic, the commander of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and that conversation took place on the 6th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to summarise that conversation for us.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our first conversation after the New Year's holiday. First we talked about a unit that the Army of Yugoslavia or, to be more precise, General Mrksic had brought to the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Perisic told me that he heard that I had decided that that unit should go back home. It was not my decision. It was General Mladic's order after I reported to him about the appearance of that unit. We continued talking and he told me, I didn't call you about that, but during the holidays, Ratko and myself - and he meant General Mladic - socialised and we discussed the aerial bombs that we could use. What do you think about those? That was the first time I heard the term, and I told him, Listen, I'm not interested in the way you Herzegovinian think. If anybody is to tell me anything about them, it will be General Mladic, not you. And that's how we left it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the record records you saying reference to "discussed the aerial bombs that we could use." Can I ask you for a bit of more detail, if there is any, about how they might use aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know whether they were actually aerial bombs. I'm not familiar with the term. Those were air fuel bombs. When I was at school, I learned about those bombs being able to change the climatic conditions. For example, in Vietnam, they could stop the rain or -- I don't know. So he used the term fuel air-bombs. I don't -- I didn't know what he was talking about. So that's why I told him what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we now look at 65 ter 1985? Again a letter addressed from Ratko Mladic to the chief of the Yugoslav Army and it bears the same date, so it has the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once you can see this document on the screen, it's in reference to a request with respect to Colonel Ivan Djokic. Can I ask you if you know him and, if you do, describe briefly who he was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, I should tell you that the previous document and this document were both issued on the 31st of May, 1995, when I was in Ostrelj, near Drvar. As for Ivan Djokic, I know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we are not asking you where you were on that date. Mr. Groome puts a question to you. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew Ivan Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his expertise or who was he in the --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an officer in the command of the air force and anti-aircraft defence of the Army of Yugoslavia. He was an expert for rocket anti-aircraft assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He helped develop the modified air-bomb, skalamerija?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see him in the theatre of war, and I believe that he helped Colonel Rajko Balac in crafting a prototype of that skalamerija contraption.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time Prosecution tenders 65 ter 1985 and 1986 as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1986 receives number P2220. And document 1985 receives number 2221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2220 and P2221 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, are you able to tell us whether these skalamerija, these modified air-bombs, were able to target precise locations or general areas?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that asset in action. Nor did I see it after it was manufactured and assembled. I only saw a model of that asset. It could not be precise, and it could not target a precise -- precisely. Like a bomb launched from an aircraft, it could target an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the placement and use of air-bombs supervised at the level of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was supervised by the chief of artillery of the Main Staff, Colonel Rajko Balac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you remind us, if we were to look at that organisational chart, in what sector would we find this person?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the staff sector, in the group of military branches or combat arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, my last series of questions is with respect to a chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that 65 ter 26001A be brought to our screen. This is a chart summarising General Milovanovic's observations regarding seven documents he was asked to review prior to giving evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while that's being called up, prior to giving evidence, were you asked to review seven documents related to humanitarian convoys and record any observations you had with respect to their authenticity and substance on a chart?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the chart that we see before us now?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is only the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we go to e-court page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you can see that, can you tell us whether you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, having completed this chart several days ago, is there anything else you would like to add to your comments before I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution now tenders 26001A into evidence. It's the chart as well as the seven documents aggregated into the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We always object to documents of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I wasn't clear, we object this time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, that's clear. I'm not seeking -- you say always of this nature. You mean charts or underlying documents or what is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this -- I mean this should then be 92 ter statement. Is it -- what kind of evidence is this? This is written statement about something. This witness is a viva voce witness, specifically for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that exclude the possibility of -- you can cross-examine the witness on it. I mean, it is a written statement to some extent, yes, but perhaps then Mr. Groome -- if Mr. Groome would ask the witness whether he gave his comments to the best of his knowledge and -- I mean, is a viva voce witness per se excluded from any written statement given for very practical reasons? I mean, that's my question, procedural question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For us, yes. If you rule differently, then it might affect our Defence case as well. And we would object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That we might have viva voce witnesses with written statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, written statements, it is limited to -- but you'd say: We would never use a chart with any of our witnesses if we call them viva voce? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I never did it before, no. I never used these charts with any of my witnesses before, nor I saw it in any other trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The chart and the underlying documents will be MFI'd for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tendered only the chart, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, to simplify matters, we aggregated the seven documents and the chart into a single exhibit. The original exhibit had the same 65 ter number with all of those documents but without the suffix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this document will be MFI'd under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 26001A receives number P2222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2222 is admitted -- is marked for identification. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, the last question I have, I wanted to return to the topic of Directive 7 and 7/1 and give you an additional opportunity to say anything that you might want to say about them now that you've had an opportunity to look at them. So let me put essentially my question to you again. Is it your evidence that you have concluded that the absence of that offensive phrase from 7/1 that we found in Directive 7 is an indication of General Mladic's intentional withdrawal of that part of the order?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you have factual knowledge that this is true or this is a conclusion that you've drawn from looking -- your retrospective reading of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal assessment and my personal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I want to thank you for your answers to my questions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I would like to deal briefly with a procedural matter but meanwhile, before you leave the courtroom, I'd like to instruct you again not to speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. You may follow the usher and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to deliver a short decision. It might take us three minutes into the time which is not ours. Nevertheless, I already ask for the indulgence of all those assisting us. It is a decision on the five Defence requests for extensions to respond, a request which was filed on the 13th of September. Having considered the current work-load of the defence and the volume and complexity of the evidence proffered in each of the relevant Prosecution's motions, as well as the Prosecution's standing submission that it will not object to any reasonable requests for extensions, the Chamber decides as follows: For the Prosecution's motion to admit the evidence of Witness RM218 and RM269, the Chamber grants an additional 14 days to respond, setting the new deadline on the 27th of September. For the Prosecution's motion to admit evidence from the bar table with regard to military justice, the Chamber grants an additional 35 days to respond, setting a new deadline of the 18th of October. For the Prosecution's motion to admit evidence from the bar table with regard to the municipalities component of the case, the Chamber grants an additional 65 days to respond, setting the new deadline on the 18th of November. For the Prosecution's 37th 92 bis motion, the Chamber grants an additional 14 days to respond, setting the new deadline of the 27th September. And the last one: For the Prosecution's 36th 92 bis motion, the Chamber first notes that the response was due on the 12th of September but that the Defence did not file its request for extension until the 13th of September. However, on an exceptional basis, the Chamber will allow the request and hereby grants an additional 30 days to respond, setting the new deadline of the 14th of October. Finally, the Chamber notes with some concern the Defence submission that it has been the guidance of the Chamber that bar table motions must be limited to only ten documents and that the Chamber has relaxed this guidance to permit the Prosecution to do as it wishes. The Chamber takes this opportunity to clarify for the Defence that it has never been the guidance of this Chamber that bar table motions be strictly limited to ten documents and that where the Chamber has given guidance, it has been an expression of the Chamber's preferences with regard to the volume and focus of proffered evidence so as not to not unnecessarily burden the Chamber or the evidentiary record and not, as the Defence suggests, to protect or promote the interest of one party over another. The Chamber might find it helpful in this regard to revisit -- I misread. The Defence might find it helpful in this regard to revisit the Chamber's guidance of the 9th of July, 2012, where it clearly stated that it would take a flexible approach in such matters and that what was most important was the focused presentation of evidence and not any precise limitation on the number of tendered exhibits. The Chamber hopes the Defence will keep this in mind when making future submissions on whether or to what extent the Chamber's guidance has been followed. I apologise for those assisting us for going beyond the time. We adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 19th of September, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of September, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
